Marguerite had run the small publishing house for eleven years, and she still opened the office herself on Mondays. The routine never varied. She unlocked the street door, filled the kettle, and read the weekend correspondence on the old desktop while the radiator clicked and the printer warmed itself with a series of complaints. By half past eight the editors had arrived, coats still damp from the rain, and the weekly meeting began with the same question: which manuscripts had survived the slush pile.

The slush pile occupied two shelves in the storage room, and its contents were catalogued in a ledger that nobody trusted. Three hundred and forty submissions had come in since January, most of them novels, a handful of memoirs, and one persistent poet who sent the same sequence of sonnets every six weeks with a different covering letter. Edith read the poetry. She had a theory that the covering letter told you more about the writer than the poems did, and she defended that theory at every meeting, usually at length.

This week the agenda had three items. The first was the autumn catalogue, which the sales director wanted to shrink from twenty titles to fourteen. The second was a dispute with the printer over paper stock, since the last delivery had arrived with a watermark that showed through on every second page. The third was the retirement of Douglas, who had handled production for thirty-one years and held opinions about paper that he considered non-negotiable. Douglas sat at the end of the table with a mug of tea and a folder of samples, and he waited until the catalogue discussion had exhausted itself before he said anything at all.

'Fourteen titles,' he said eventually, 'means fourteen chances instead of twenty. It also means we print more copies of each one, and the warehouse holds what we print. I have no objection to the number. I object to the schedule, which gives production eleven weeks for a job that has always taken fourteen.'

Marguerite wrote the objection on the whiteboard, where it joined a list of other objections from previous meetings, some of them added in the spring. The list was long enough that the marker had begun to squeak. Nobody minded, because the list was also the closest thing the company had to a plan.

The conversation moved to the printer. The watermark, it emerged, came from a paper mill that had changed suppliers in the summer, and the fault lay with a coating applied too thinly on the second side. The printer offered a discount. Douglas offered a lecture on the history of coated stock, which was more interesting than it sounds. By midday they had agreed to accept the discount and to test three alternative papers on the next reprint, provided the samples arrived before the end of the month.

After lunch Edith raised the question of the poet, whose submissions had been rejected nine times. She proposed that they publish a single sequence in the winter anthology and write a proper letter explaining why the rest did not suit the list. The editors argued about this for twenty minutes, not because they disagreed, but because arguing was how they reached agreement. In the end the proposal passed with one abstention, the abstention being Douglas, who claimed that poetry was outside his remit and that he had enough trouble with paper.

At three the meeting ended and the office emptied. Marguerite remained to clear the cups. Leaving, she stopped at the production desk, took a tape measure from the drawer, and asked the warehouse foreman to record the distance between the two storage shelves, since the flat files would have to be moved north of the loading bay before the new stock arrived.
